desc:
An array is a mountain if it has at least 3 elements and there is an index p with 0 < p < n - 1 such that nums[0] < nums[1] < ... < nums[p] and nums[p] > nums[p + 1] > ... > nums[n - 1].

Given a mountain array nums, return the index p of its peak. Do better than a linear scan: an O(log n) solution exists.

For example, in [1, 4, 9, 6, 2] the peak is at index 2.
constraints: nums is guaranteed to be a mountain array
hints: Scanning for the maximum is O(n). What does the mountain shape tell you about the elements to the left or right of any position?
Look at one position mid and its right neighbour. If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], are you on the rising slope or the falling slope? Where can the peak be?

Keep the range [lo, hi] that must contain the peak. If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1] the peak is strictly right of mid, so lo = mid + 1; otherwise the peak is at mid or left of it, so hi = mid. Stop when lo == hi.
editorial: The question 'is position i still climbing?', that is nums[i] < nums[i + 1], is true for every index before the peak and false for the peak and everything after it. A predicate that flips exactly once is what a binary search needs.

Maintain lo = 0, hi = n - 1. While lo < hi, take mid = (lo + hi) // 2; mid + 1 is always in range because mid < hi. If the slope is rising, the peak is right of mid, so move lo to mid + 1. Otherwise mid could itself be the peak, so keep it and set hi = mid. The range halves each step and ends on the peak.
That is O(log n) time and O(1) space. Because all neighbouring values differ (strict slopes), there is no plateau that could make the test ambiguous.
